newsitem.title: USA: Bell Atlantic, SBC defend mergers.
newsitem.headline: Bell Atlantic, SBC defend mergers.

text.p: Bell Atlantic Corp and SBC Communications Inc denied Wednesday their proposed mergers with rival Baby Bells would lead to bigger local phone monopolies that would stamp out competitors.

Executives from the two Baby Bells also complained to a Senate panel that new Federal Communications Commission rules were hampering -- instead of hastening -- the opening of local phone markets to competition.
But executives from long-distance carriers such as MCI Communications Corp told the judiciary committee they supported the FCC rules and that the Bells were dragging their feet in implementing them.
And they charged that the $22 billion Bell Atlantic Corp-NYNEX Corp. merger and the $16.7 billion SBC-Pacific Telesis Group deal raise antitrust concerns and should be blocked by regulators.
"The proposed mergers are very troubling and should be opposed," MCI General Counsel Michael Salsbury told senators.

He warned that the transactions would hurt development of competition in the local phone market in each of the existing seven Baby Bell regions. And he said the deals would enable the Bells to "leverage their local phone monopolies to gain market power in the long-distance market."

The committee hearing follows passage earlier this year of the landmark telecommunications law designed to encourage local and long-distance phone companies, cable-television operators and others to invade each others' turf.
The proposed mergers of the Baby Bells, along with the recent proposed $9.2 billion acquisition of MFS Communications Co. Inc. by WORLDCOM Inc., have occurred in wake of the law.

"The merger raises no concerns under this nation's antitrust laws, and is in the interest of the customers, employees, and shareholders of both companies," SBC Executive Vice President James Ellis said of SBC's proposed deal.
He said the deal would benefit consumers by allowing the merged companies to offer more products and services at competitive prices.
Ellis and Bell Atlantic Vice President James Young also indicated that their companies have no strong enthusiasm to challenge rival Baby Bells head on in local markets.
Democratic lawmakers -- echoing long-distance executives -- voiced doubts about the mergers, saying the recent string of Baby Bell deals have done little to promote competition.
"Instead of seeing new entrants into every market, we are seeing old monopolies getting bigger and expanding their reach," said Sen. Patrick Leahy, a Vermont Democrat.
Meanwhile, the Bells have challenged in court the FCC's "interconnection" rules for opening the local phone market and are seeking to overturn the regulations.

"The FCC has gone far beyond the limited role Congress prescribed for it," SBC's Ellis told lawmakers. He argued the rules leave virtually nothing for arbitration between the Bells and competitors attempting to enter their territory.
And he said the FCC "preempted the role preserved for the states by Congress, and has, in essence, 'nationalized' control of the local exchange industry."
